## 1. Walking downhill

Training a model means finding weights that make the loss small. Gradient descent gets there in small moves. At each step it checks which way the loss slopes and steps the other way [RK3 s.12] [LT4 p.5].

```symbols
- RK3: w
  LT4: \theta
  means: the weights
- RK3: \alpha
  LT4: \eta
  means: the step size, also called the learning rate
- RK3: \nabla L
  LT4: \nabla J
  means: the slope of the loss
```

```formula
n: '1.1'
parts:
- tex: w_{new}
  says: the new weights
- tex: '='
- tex: w
  says: the weights now
- tex: '-'
- tex: \alpha
  says: the step size
- tex: \nabla L(w)
  says: the slope of the loss
beneath: 'In LT''s notes: $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \nabla J(\theta)$'
glance: One step of gradient descent
cite: [RK3 s.12, LT4 p.5]
```

The weights $w$ move against the slope, by an amount set by the step size $\alpha$. The step size is the one part chosen by hand, which is why the next figure is about it [RK3 s.14].

> [!key]
> Each step moves the weights a little way downhill, and the step size decides how far.

```widget
n: '1.1'
shell: slider and plot
model: gd curve
title: Choosing the step size
says: Pick a step size and watch eight steps on a bowl-shaped loss.
params:
  loss: [1, -6, 10]
  start: -1
  rates: [0.1, 0.3, 0.9, 1.05]
  rate: 0.3
  steps: 8
  flat: 0.01
  view: [-2, 8]
guess: With a step size of 1.05, does it settle, crawl or run away?
cite: [RK3 s.14]
```

> [!lectures]
> - RK3: Starts at $\alpha = 0.01$ and shrinks it when the loss jumps. [RK3 s.14]
> - LT4: Halves $\eta$ every ten passes over the data. [LT4 p.6]

> [!claude]
> On a bowl shaped like this one, any step size above 1 sends each step farther from the bottom than the last. Real losses aren't perfect bowls, so the safe range is found by watching the loss.

> [!disagrees] On [LT4 p.7]
> The update is written with a plus sign there. Stepping with the slope climbs uphill, so the sign should be a minus, as on [LT4 p.5].

> [!brief]
> - Each step moves the weights against the slope of the loss.
> - The step size is the one part set by hand.
> - Too small crawls. Too large overshoots and can blow up.

## 2. When to stop

The steps get shorter as the slope flattens near the bottom. Training stops when the slope is close to zero or the loss stops improving [RK3 s.15] [LT4 p.6].

> [!definition] Converged
> The loss has stopped going down in any way that matters, so more steps change little. [RK3 s.15]

> [!brief]
> - The slope shrinks near the bottom, so the steps do too.
> - Stop when the loss stops improving.

# Learn

```warmup
- q: Which way does the slope of the loss point?
  a: Uphill, toward a larger loss.
  cite: [RK3 s.13]
```

```guess
- '1.1'
```

```explain
q: Explain gradient descent to a friend in two sentences, without the formula.
takeaways:
- It takes small steps downhill on the loss.
- The step size decides how far each step goes.
```

```cards
- id: gd-1
  kind: recall
  q: 'Explain what each part of the update rule in formula 1.1 does.'
  a: 'The weights move against the slope of the loss, by an amount the step size sets. Repeating it walks downhill.'
  cite: [RK3 s.12]
- id: gd-2
  kind: why
  q: 'What goes wrong when the step size is too small, and when it''s too large?'
  a: 'Too small and training crawls. Too large and each step overshoots the bottom, so the loss bounces or grows.'
  cite: [RK3 s.14]
- id: gd-3
  kind: across courses
  q: 'Read formula 1.1 in LT''s symbols. What are $\theta$ and $\eta$?'
  a: '$\theta$ is the weights and $\eta$ is the step size. LT writes the loss as $J$.'
  cite: [LT4 p.5]
- id: gd-4
  kind: why
  q: 'Why does gradient descent step against the slope and not with it?'
  a: 'The slope points uphill. Stepping the other way lowers the loss, at least for a small step.'
  cite: [RK3 s.13]
- id: gd-5
  kind: across courses
  q: 'How do the two lecturers change the step size during training?'
  a: 'RK starts small and shrinks it when the loss jumps. LT halves it every ten passes.'
  cite: [LT4 p.6]
```
